prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

All my life I was face to face with her, at meal-times, by the fire, even in the ultimate intimacies of the bed. You could have asked, then, for information about her? There was a room apart she kept herself in, teasing me by leading me to its glass door, only to confront me with my reflection. I learned from her even so. Walking her shore I found things cast up from her depths that spoke to me of another order, worshipper as I was of untamed nature. She fetched her treasures from art’s storehouse: pieces of old lace, delicate as frost; china from a forgotten period; a purse more valuable than anything it could contain. Coming in from the fields with my offering of flowers I found her garden had forestalled me in providing civilities for my desk. ‘Tell me about life,’ I would say, ‘you who were its messenger in the delivery of our child.’ Her eyes had a fine shame, remembering her privacy being invaded from further off than she expected. ‘Do you think death is the end?’ frivolously I would ask her. I recall now the swiftness of its arrival wrenching her lip down, and how the upper remained firm, reticent as the bud that is the precursor of the flower.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The narrator lived in constant intimacy with the woman yet felt unable to truly know her inner self.
- The woman maintained a private inner world that the narrator could approach but never fully enter.
- The narrator learned about her indirectly through the refined objects and gestures she valued.
- The contrast between the narrator’s love of untamed nature and her appreciation for art and civility reveals their different sensibilities.
- The narrator recalls asking her about life and death, remembering her guarded, dignified response to mortality.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The passage explores the speaker’s lifelong attempt to understand an intimate yet elusive woman, using reflective memories and symbolic contrasts between nature, art, birth, and death. It reveals that despite constant closeness, her inner life remains partly inaccessible, underscoring the mystery at the heart of love, identity, and mortality.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: All, You, There

outputs.L1:
All my life, I stood face to face with her: at mealtimes, by the fire, even in the ultimate intimacies of the bed. Could I, then, have asked her for information about herself? There was a room apart in which she kept herself, teasing me by leading me to its glass door, only to confront me with my own reflection.

Even so, I learned from her. Walking her shore, I found things cast up from her depths that spoke to me of another order, worshipper though I was of untamed nature. She fetched her treasures from art’s storehouse: pieces of old lace, delicate as frost; china from a forgotten period; a purse more valuable than anything it could contain. Coming in from the fields with my offering of flowers, I found that her garden had already forestalled me, providing civilities for my desk.

“Tell me about life,” I would say, “you who were its messenger in the delivery of our child.” Her eyes held a fine shame, remembering how her privacy had been invaded from farther off than she had expected. “Do you think death is the end?” I would ask her, frivolously. I recall now the swiftness of its arrival wrenching her lip downward, and how the upper one remained firm, reticent as the bud that precedes the flower.
outputs.L2:
Throughout my life, she was always before me: across the table at meals, beside the hearth, and even in the deepest closeness of our shared bed. Could I, therefore, have questioned her and learned who she was? She seemed to reserve some separate chamber within herself, drawing me toward its glass door in a kind of provocation, then leaving me to meet only my own image there.

Still, I learned from her in other ways. As I wandered along the edge of her being, I discovered objects thrown up from hidden depths, signs of a different kind of order, though I myself revered wild, uncontrolled nature. Her riches came from the treasury of art: antique lace as fragile and intricate as frost, porcelain belonging to some vanished age, and a purse worth more than anything it might ever hold.

When I returned from the fields carrying flowers as my tribute, I would find that her own garden had already supplied refined offerings for my writing table. “Tell me what life is,” I would ask her, “since you served as its envoy when our child was born.” In her eyes there would appear a delicate embarrassment, as though she remembered that her most private self had been entered from a greater distance than she had imagined possible.

“And do you believe death is the finish?” I would ask lightly. Now I remember how quickly the thought of it came upon her, pulling down her lower lip, while the upper one stayed composed and silent, closed like the bud that comes before the flower.
outputs.L3:
Although the narrator lived in constant intimacy with the woman, he remained aware of a profound distance between them. Their closeness did not give him full access to her inner life. He could share her daily surroundings, observe her habits, and feel the force of his affection for her, yet he still sensed that the deepest part of her remained beyond his reach. This creates a tension between physical or emotional nearness and true understanding: he is close to her, but he cannot completely know her.

The woman is presented as someone who preserves a private inner world. The narrator may approach this world through conversation, memory, and observation, but he can never fully enter it. Her self-possession gives her an air of mystery and dignity. She does not surrender herself entirely to explanation, nor does she allow her thoughts and feelings to become completely transparent. This privacy is not portrayed as emptiness or coldness, but as a sign of depth. She has an interior life that exists independently of the narrator’s desire to understand it.

As a result, the narrator comes to know her indirectly. He reads her character through the things she values: refined objects, cultivated gestures, forms of beauty shaped by taste and civilization. Her surroundings, her manners, and her preferences become clues to her personality. Rather than revealing herself through direct confession, she is revealed through the atmosphere she creates around herself. The narrator interprets her through details—through art, elegance, restraint, and the quiet significance of chosen objects.

This indirect knowledge also highlights the difference between their sensibilities. The narrator is drawn to untamed nature, to what is wild, immediate, and unshaped by human refinement. The woman, by contrast, finds meaning in art, civility, and cultivated beauty. Their contrast suggests two different ways of encountering the world. He values the raw force of natural life, while she values form, grace, and the human capacity to transform experience into art. This difference does not necessarily separate them completely, but it marks the limits of their mutual understanding.

The narrator’s memory of asking her about life and death further reveals her character. When confronted with mortality, she responds with reserve and dignity. She does not collapse into fear, nor does she offer an easy or sentimental answer. Her guarded response suggests both vulnerability and strength. She acknowledges death without fully exposing her feelings about it. In remembering this moment, the narrator recognizes again the mystery at the center of her being: even in the face of the most universal human question, she remains composed, private, and partly unknowable.
outputs.L4:
The passage reflects on the speaker’s lifelong effort to understand a woman who has remained both deeply familiar and strangely unreachable. She is not a distant figure in any ordinary sense; on the contrary, she has lived close to him, sharing the ordinary intimacies of time, memory, and daily life. Yet this closeness does not lead to complete knowledge. The more the speaker recalls, observes, and reflects, the more he becomes aware of a hidden inwardness that he cannot fully enter. She is present beside him, but part of her remains elsewhere.

The speaker’s memories move between moments of tenderness, wonder, and uncertainty. He seems to search the past for clues, returning to scenes that might explain who she is: gestures, expressions, silences, changes in mood, and fragments of shared experience. These memories are not merely personal recollections; they become a way of asking larger questions about human identity. Can one person ever truly know another? Does love bring understanding, or does it simply make mystery more intense?

Throughout the passage, the woman is associated with symbolic contrasts. Nature suggests vitality, instinct, growth, and change, while art suggests form, interpretation, and the human desire to preserve or make meaning. Birth evokes beginnings, creation, and the promise of life, while death introduces limitation, disappearance, and the final unknowability of another person. These oppositions deepen the speaker’s meditation. The woman seems connected to all of them at once: she is living and mortal, natural and self-fashioned, intimate and unknowable.

The speaker’s tone is reflective and searching rather than certain. He does not claim to have solved the mystery of her being. Instead, he recognizes that his long closeness to her has not erased the distance between them. This distance is not simply a failure of communication; it is part of what it means to love another person. Love brings two lives together, but it does not make them identical. Each person remains enclosed within a private consciousness that even the most devoted companion can only partly imagine.

In this way, the passage becomes more than a portrait of one woman. It is also a meditation on the limits of knowledge, the nature of intimacy, and the inevitability of mortality. The speaker’s inability to fully understand her does not diminish his attachment; if anything, it gives that attachment its depth. Her mystery becomes central to his love, reminding him that every human being contains an inner world that cannot be completely possessed, explained, or translated.

Ultimately, the passage reveals that the woman’s elusiveness is not an obstacle to meaning but the very source of it. She remains close, beloved, and vividly remembered, yet never entirely known. Through this tension, the speaker confronts the deepest truths of human relationship: that love is bound to mystery, that identity exceeds interpretation, and that mortality makes every attempt at understanding both urgent and incomplete.
outputs.L5:
**All You Need Is There**

All around you, there are moments waiting to be noticed. There is beauty in the quiet morning, in the sound of laughter, and in the small steps you take each day. You may not always see it, but there is strength within you and hope ahead of you.

All challenges can teach you something. All dreams begin with a single thought. All progress starts when you decide to keep going, even when the road feels uncertain.

Remember, you are not alone. There is always a new chance, a new path, and a new reason to believe. All you need to do is look around, take a breath, and trust that there is something good waiting for you.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short, introspective literary monologue in the style of early 20th-century modernist prose, narrated by a widower reflecting on his wife, marriage, intimacy, art, nature, childbirth, and death.
counterfactuals.output:
How strange, that a life may remain in a room after the body has been carried out of it.

Her shawl hangs still upon the chair, collapsed as though it too has learned fatigue. In the mornings the light comes in—thin, judicial, indifferent—and lays itself along the floorboards where her feet once moved, quick at first, then slow, then with that guarded heaviness of the last months when the child pressed downward and the whole house seemed to listen for her breath. I had thought marriage a joining, a noble arrangement of souls; but it was more bodily than that, more humble, made of hairpins, warm linen, the small blue vein at her temple, the smell of milk, rain, soap, and sleep.

I loved her least when I tried to make her into art. Sitting by the window, her head bent over sewing, she became for me composition, line, tenderness arranged by light. How cruel the eye can be, even in devotion. She would look up and laugh—knowing, perhaps, that I had taken her from herself and placed her in some private gallery of mine. Yet she returned, always returned, to the world: to boiling water, to the cry of crows, to the earth darkening under spring rain. She belonged more truly to these than to my thoughts.

When the child was born, I understood nothing. There was blood, and a sound like an animal caught in a thicket, and then that astonishing cry—thin, offended, alive. Her face, emptied and radiant, frightened me. It was as if she had gone down into some black country and come back carrying fire. I stood beside her uselessly, with my clean hands.

Now she is gone again into that country, and this time has not returned.

Outside, the garden renews itself with an almost vulgar confidence. Buds open. Worms work invisibly in the soaked beds. The pear tree, which she planted crookedly and defended against my corrections, has flowered white as bone. Nature is not consolation. It is continuance, and continuance is sometimes the sharpest grief.

At night I lie on my half of the bed, faithful to a border no one enforces, and feel the vastness of her absence beside me. Intimacy, I see now, was not the being known, but the being witnessed in one’s vanishing—day by day, gesture by gesture—until death merely completed what love had long rehearsed.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a dense poetic paragraph about a man trying and failing to truly know his wife, using images of mirrors, shorelines, old lace, china, flowers, and the expression on her face when death is mentioned.
counterfactuals.output: He spent his life approaching her as one approaches a mirror in a dim room, believing the nearness of his breath on the glass would clarify her, yet finding only his own weathered face returned in fragments beside the pale, withheld country of hers; she was all shorelines to him, receding whenever he named the tide, leaving shells of laughter, a ribbon of old lace, the blue crack in a china cup, flowers arranged with such grave tenderness they seemed less alive than commemorative. He learned the perfumes she favored, the hour she opened the curtains, the small ceremonies of sugar and spoon, the way her hands smoothed linen as if quieting a child or a ghost, but never the hidden province from which these gestures came. Sometimes, at dinner, when death was mentioned lightly—someone’s uncle, a distant funeral, a phrase in the paper—her face would alter: not with fear, not sorrow exactly, but with a sudden inward brightness, as if a door had opened on a shore he could not see, where mirrors bloomed like cold flowers and the delicate lace of the waves kept lifting and erasing her name.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a Virginia Woolf–like passage in which a husband recalls his dead wife as both familiar and unknowable, contrasting his love of wild nature with her refined domestic treasures.
counterfactuals.output:
He had thought, when she was living, that he knew her—as one knows the shape of a room in the dark, the chair to be avoided, the table-edge, the window where the night gathers. Her step upon the stair, the slight pause before she entered, the way her hand went, not uncertainly but meditatively, to the clasp at her throat: these things had seemed to him the very alphabet of her being. Yet now that she was dead she withdrew, not into obscurity merely, but into a kind of brightness, like a figure seen across water, distinct and unrecoverable.

How often he had come in smelling of rain, of crushed fern, of the sour sweetness of marshland, with burrs on his coat and clay on his boots, exulting in the wind that had beaten against him on the headland, in the gulls crying savagely over the grey heave of the sea. He had loved the roughness of things—the torn bark of pines, the black pools under rocks, the sudden flight of deer through bracken. Nature, to him, had been truest where it was least arranged.

And she—how delicately she had set herself against all that wild profusion. Not coldly; no, never coldly. But she had gathered beauty as one gathers a flame in a lamp: the porcelain bowl on the mantel, painted with minute blue reeds; the little ivory fan; the silver box that held nothing, or only the faint powdery scent of vanished letters; the embroidered cushions whose stitches seemed to him, once, a frivolous patience. He had smiled at these treasures, tenderly perhaps, perhaps condescendingly. Now they accused him by remaining.

For there they were still, composed and mute, while she was nowhere. Or rather she was everywhere among them and yet not contained by them: in the gleam on the teacup’s rim, in the folded shawl, in the empty chair angled toward the fire. Familiar—yes, more familiar than his own hands. And yet what had she thought, sitting there while the rain pressed its face to the glass and he spoke of storms, cliffs, the fierce freedom of the open fields? Had she listened with love, with weariness, with some inward smile he had never learned to read?

He saw then that marriage had been not possession, not even knowledge, but a long companionship beside a locked door. She had given him years, glances, habits, the touch of her sleeve passing him in the hall. She had kept, behind all that, her own still country: furnished, luminous, inaccessible.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an elegiac prose fragment from the perspective of a husband remembering conversations with his wife about life and death, ending with a close observation of her lips and emotional restraint.
counterfactuals.output:
We used to speak of death in the ordinary hours, as if it were another household matter to be set beside bread, weather, the late bills on the table. She would bring it up while folding linen or standing at the window with the evening light caught in her hair, and I, coward that I was, would answer lightly, trying to turn the thought aside. But she never spoke of it morbidly. To her, death was not a door slammed shut, but a room one entered after long preparation, with the hope that those left behind would continue to light the lamps.

“Life asks so much of us,” she once said, “and then asks us to let it go.”

I remember laughing then, not because it was funny, but because I could not bear the gravity of her voice. She looked at me with that patient sorrow she had for my evasions, and I understood that she was already braver than I would ever be. She was teaching me, even then, how to lose her.

Now the rooms keep her words more faithfully than I do. They return them at dusk, when the chairs darken and the glass reflects no one I want to see. I hear again her quiet insistence that love is not defeated by absence, only changed into a form more difficult to hold. I had thought our conversations were about some distant country. I did not know she was drawing me a map.

In her final days she spoke less, but her silence was not empty. It gathered around us like snow. I sat beside her and tried to be worthy of the calm she had spent a lifetime making. Her mouth, once so quick to smile at my foolishness, had grown pale with effort; the lips were slightly parted, dry at the edges, as if holding back one last tenderness. I did not weep. I watched them tremble, and kept still.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a literary imitation of British modernist fiction: a narrator speaks of living “face to face” with his wife yet being kept outside her inner room, discovering clues to her soul through objects, childbirth, and mortality.
counterfactuals.output:
We lived, my wife and I, face to face; that is to say, we breakfasted across the same white cloth, heard the same gulls quarrelling beyond the chimneys, grew old beneath the same weather. Yet there was always, behind her eyes, a room into which I was not admitted. I might stand at the threshold (for marriage gives one that much license), might see the firelight move upon the wall within, might hear some chair drawn softly back; but when I entered, it was only the outer chamber I found—the smile, the hand laid on mine, the little practical questions about letters, servants, trains.

So I became a collector of evidences. Not of facts, for facts are blunt instruments, and she was made of shades; but of small abandoned things. A glove turned inside out on the hall table, retaining the shape of her fingers as a shell retains the sea. A blue ribbon in a drawer, faded at the fold, which she denied remembering and yet touched, before putting it away, with a tenderness one does not waste on ribbon. Books with their pages cut to the end, though she had claimed not to read now; and in the margins, once or twice, a vertical stroke, severe as a suppressed cry.

When our first child was born I thought—foolishly, greedily—that the door would open. For surely in pain, in that savage business by which the body is made public, the soul must become visible too. I saw her face then, not as a husband sees, but as a man shipwrecked sees a light on the coast: far, absolute, belonging to another order. She cried out; she cursed me, perhaps; she called for her mother, dead fifteen years. And when the child was laid beside her, purple, astonishing, clenched against the world, she looked not at me but beyond me, with an expression of recognition. As if someone had returned whom she alone expected.

Afterwards the house filled with milk, linen, whispers, the sour-sweet odour of new life. I found her hairpins everywhere, as though she had been dismantled in passing from room to room. On the nursery chair lay her shawl, and beneath it a letter never posted. There was nothing in it—nothing that would satisfy a court, a biographer, a jealous man. Only: “I am afraid that what I am cannot be given, even to those I love.” No name. No signature. The sentence seemed at once a confession and a door closed quietly.

Years loosened us. Children ran through us like weather through trees and were gone. Her face, which I had once studied for disclosures, became lined with its own reticence; mine, I suppose, grew patient from failure. We sat together in the evenings, closer than before, and spoke less. Sometimes I believed that the inner room had vanished, or that I had invented it in the arrogance of youth, wanting possession where companionship was the only gift offered. Then she would turn her head at the sound of rain, or pause with a cup halfway to her lips, and an immense distance would open in the gesture.

In her last illness she permitted me every intimacy but the one I desired. I lifted her, fed her, watched the bones arrange themselves under the skin. Death, which strips so much, did not strip that. Rather it made the hidden place more radiant, like a lamp seen behind thick curtains at dusk. On the final morning she asked for the little box in her dressing-table. I brought it, thinking at last—letters, a portrait, some key.

Inside were absurd trifles: the blue ribbon, a pebble from a beach I had forgotten, a child’s first tooth, two theatre tickets, a pressed violet, brown as old smoke. She smiled at my bewilderment.

“You see,” she said.

But I did not see. Or only then began to see: that a soul is not a chamber to be entered, nor a document to be read by the lawful owner of a life lived adjacent to it. It is rather the pattern made by what it has touched and relinquished; the warmth left in a glove; the margin marked beside a sentence; the cry in childbirth that summons the dead; the box of foolish relics carried, secretly, to the edge.

We had lived face to face. That was true. And perhaps no one is granted more.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
